leaves.title: Completing a personal information form
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll practice writing the kind of personal information you're asked for constantly — on a form, an online account, or a booking.

Common form fields: first name, last name, nationality, address, zip code, age, marital status (married or single), phone number (home and cell), email address.

A few formatting rules that matter for forms:

• First name and last name are always capitalized: Maria Santos, not maria santos.
• Nationality words are also capitalized: American, Brazilian.
• An address usually includes a street number and name, city, and state: 15 Hill Drive, Los Angeles, CA.
• Phone numbers are usually written in groups, e.g. 415-555-0132.
• Email addresses are always lowercase and have no spaces: maria.santos@email.com.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to fill out a full personal information form correctly and confidently.
examples: First name: Maria — Last name: Santos
Address: 15 Hill Drive, Los Angeles, CA — Zip code: 90041
commonMistakes: Don't write your name in all lowercase or all capitals on a form — use a capital letter only at the start of each name.
Don't add spaces inside an email address or phone number.
Nationality words are capitalized just like country names: 'american' is wrong — write 'American'.

exercises.title: Complete the form fields
exercises.instructions: Write the correctly formatted answer for each form field.

questions.prompt: Write your first name with correct capitalization: (e.g. answer for 'liam')
Write this phone number correctly grouped: 4155550132
Write this email address correctly: LIAM.CHEN@EMAIL.COM
Write this nationality with correct capitalization: (e.g. answer for 'american')

exercises.title: Choose the correctly formatted answer
exercises.instructions: Choose the version that is correctly formatted for a form.

questions.prompt: Which email address is correctly formatted?
Which phone number is correctly grouped?
Which form field asks whether you are married or single?
Which is a complete, correctly formatted address?

leaves.title: Writing an invitation email
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to write a short, informal email inviting someone to do something — a genuinely useful everyday writing task.

A simple structure for an invitation email:

• Greeting: Hi [name],
• The invitation: Would you like to come to...? / I'm having a... Would you like to join us?
• The details: day, time, place
• A closing line: Let me know! / Hope you can come!
• Sign-off: See you soon, [your name]

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to write a clear, friendly invitation email with all the necessary details.
examples: Hi Sam, Would you like to come to a party at my house on Saturday at 8:00? Let me know! See you soon, Alex
Hi Noor, I'm having dinner on Friday. Would you like to come? Hope you can come!
commonMistakes: Don't forget to include all three key details — day, time, and place — or your friend won't know when or where to go.
An informal invitation email should sound friendly and casual, not like a formal business letter.

exercises.title: Complete the invitation email
exercises.instructions: Complete each missing part of the invitation email.

questions.prompt: Would you like to ___ to a party on Saturday? (verb)
___ know if you can come! (closing request)

exercises.title: Choose the missing detail
exercises.instructions: Choose which key detail is missing from each invitation.

questions.prompt: 'Would you like to come to my party?' is missing...
options: a greeting, day, time, and place

questions.prompt: An invitation email should always include...

leaves.title: Writing a short blog post about yesterday
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to write a short, personal blog-style post describing what you did yesterday — practicing the simple past in a real writing format.

A simple structure:

• Start with a general statement: Yesterday was a busy/quiet/great day.
• Describe your day in time order: In the morning, I... In the afternoon, I... In the evening, I...
• Use time-order words: first, then, after that, finally
• End with a short opinion: It was a good day! / I was very tired by the evening.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to write a clear, well-organized short post describing a day using the simple past.
examples: Yesterday was a busy day. In the morning, I went to work. In the afternoon, I had a class. In the evening, I cooked dinner and watched TV. It was a good day!
First, I got up at seven. Then, I had breakfast. After that, I went for a run.
commonMistakes: Don't switch tenses randomly — a post about yesterday should stay in the simple past throughout.
Don't just list actions without time-order words (first, then, after that) — they help the reader follow the sequence.

exercises.title: Complete the blog post
exercises.instructions: Complete each missing part of the blog post about yesterday.

questions.prompt: ___, I went to work. (in the morning)
I got up, ___ I had breakfast. (next)
It ___ a great day! (simple past of be)

exercises.title: Put the events in time order
exercises.instructions: Choose which event should come first in a blog post about yesterday.

options: In the morning, I had breakfast.
In the evening, I went to bed.
